This compendium of traditional law (*smṛtinibandha*) titled *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by the great scholar named Śrī Hemādri, who was endowed with profound intelligence, is divided into sections on Vows (*vrata*), Gifts (*dāna*), and Pilgrimage Sites (*tīrtha*). Among these, the section on Vows and the section on Gifts [have been published] by the President of the Society...
It was printed through the editorial efforts of the late Bharatacandra Śiromaṇi Mahodaya, the foremost among scholars; subsequently, upon the passing of those Mahodayas into the other world,
the Śrāddhakhaṇḍa contained within the Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa was [completed] by the President of the Society.

It has been printed with the approval of Mahodaya and through our own efforts at collation. In the process of collation, three manuscript copies served as our aids. Two of them, marked Ka and Kha, were obtained from Vārāṇasī, and one, marked Ga, was obtained from the Calcutta Sanskrit College.
Obtained from a library; among these three manuscripts, two are correct and one is incorrect.

Regarding that triad of manuscripts in which doubt arose, it has been corrected with the assistance of the Smṛtis and nibandhas of Śūlapāṇi, Manu, and others. Subsequently, [the portion] contained within the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa*—
"The printing of the Kālakhaṇḍa will take place;
it is expected that this publication will be of benefit to great souls."
Furthermore, it is reported that Hemādri was a southern Brāhmaṇa belonging to the Vātsa gotra;
Kāmadeva, Vāsudeva, and Vāmanadeva were his father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, respectively. He [Hemādri] was indeed a Mahārājādhirāja born of the Yādava lineage residing at Devagiri.
Mahādeva was a scholar who presided over all branches of learning, O King;
he indeed composed [this work] in the Śaka year measured by the mountains (seven), the directions (ten), and the moon (one).
Hemādri, however, was certainly his contemporary; so, enough of this.
Of Śrī Yajñośravaraśarman; of Śrī Kāmākhyānāthaśarman.
In the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*,
in the first chapter, the section on the praise of Vājasaneya.
In the second [chapter], the section on the *pipīyā*;
in the third, the section on the *devatāniyama*;
and in the fourth, the section on the description of the *ājya* regions.
In the fifth [chapter], the section on the determination of the time for distribution;
in the sixth, the definition of the Brāhmaṇa; and in the seventh, the section on the definition of those who are to be excluded from the assembly.
In the ninth [chapter], the section on determining the substances to be thrown into the fire;
in the tenth, the section on technical definitions (paribhāṣā).
On the eleventh day he halted his chariot; on the thirteenth day, at the afternoon [session], he completed the sacrifice.
In the fourteenth [chapter], the section on those who advocate for the circumambulation;
in the fifteenth, the commencement of the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa-dāna*),
and the definition of items such as those that have been sprinkled with water (*prokṣita*).
In this [work],
the eighth section is the method for the performance of the śrāddha; the nineteenth is the method for the performance of the pilgrimage to sacred sites (tīrtha-yātrā).

The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a lotus flower that has not yet opened its petals; the person who is like a lotus flower that has opened its petals but is still covered by water; the person who is like a lotus flower that has opened its petals and is above the water; and the person who is like a lotus flower that has burst through the water and stands out, no longer touched by the water. And how, monks, is one a person like a lotus flower that has not yet opened its petals? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of lust for sensual pleasures, with a mind full of ill will, and with a mind full of dullness and drowsiness. He does not understand as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’;

he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. He does not understand as it really is: ‘These are the defilements’; he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the origin of the defilements’; he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of the defilements’; he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the defilements. He does not understand as it really is: ‘These are the states leading to rebirth’; he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the origin of the states leading to rebirth’; he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of the states leading to rebirth’; he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the states leading to rebirth. He does not understand as it really is: ‘These are the states leading to Nibbāna’; he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the origin of the states leading to Nibbāna’; he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of the states leading to Nibbāna’; he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the states leading to Nibbāna. Just as a lotus flower born in the water and grown in the water remains submerged within the water and does not rise above it, even so, monks, such a person dwells with a mind full of lust for sensual pleasures, with a mind full of ill will, and with a mind full of dullness and drowsiness... [as before] ...he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the states leading to Nibbāna. This, monks, is called a person who is like a lotus flower that has not yet opened its petals. And how, monks, is one a person who is like a lotus flower that has opened its petals but is still covered by water? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind free from lust for sensual pleasures, with a mind free from ill will, and with a mind free from dullness and drowsiness... [as before] ...he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the states leading to Nibbāna. Just as a lotus flower born in the water and grown in the water has opened its petals but remains covered by the water, even so, monks, such a person dwells with a mind free from lust for sensual pleasures, with a mind free from ill will, and with a mind free from dullness and drowsiness... [as before] ...he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the states leading to Nibbāna. This, monks, is called a person who is like a lotus flower that has opened its petals but is still covered by water. And how, monks, is one a person who is like a lotus flower that has opened its petals and is above the water? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind free from lust for sensual pleasures, with a mind free from ill will, and with a mind free from dullness and drowsiness... [as before] ...he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the states leading to Nibbāna. Just as a lotus flower born in the water and grown in the water has opened its petals and stands above the water, even so, monks, such a person dwells with a mind free from lust for sensual pleasures, with a mind free from ill will, and with a mind free from dullness and drowsiness... [as before] ...he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the states leading to Nibbāna. This, monks, is called a person who is like a lotus flower that has opened its petals and is above the water. And how, monks, is one a person who is like a lotus flower that has burst through the water and stands out, no longer touched by the water? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind free from lust for sensual pleasures, with a mind free from ill will, and with a mind free from dullness and drowsiness... [as before] ...he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the states leading to Nibbāna. Just as a lotus flower born in the water and grown in the water has burst through the water and stands out, no longer touched by the water, even so, monks, such a person dwells with a mind free from lust for sensual pleasures, with a mind free from ill will, and with a mind free from dullness and drowsiness... [as before] ...he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the states leading to Nibbāna. This, monks, is called a person who is like a lotus flower that has burst through the water and stands out, no longer touched by the water. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. : : :

The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four ways of entering the womb (*garbhāvakrānti*). What four? Here, monks, one person enters the womb with mindfulness and remains in the womb with mindfulness, and departs from the womb with mindfulness. This, monks, is the first way of entering the womb. Furthermore, monks, one person enters the womb without mindfulness and remains in the womb without mindfulness, but departs from the womb with mindfulness. This, monks, is the second way of entering the womb. Furthermore, monks, one person enters the womb without mindfulness and remains in the womb without mindfulness, and departs from the womb without mindfulness. This, monks, is the third way of entering the womb. Furthermore, monks, one person enters the womb without mindfulness and remains in the womb without mindfulness, and departs from the womb without mindfulness; moreover, he is obstructed by ignorance and enveloped by craving. This, monks, is the fourth way of entering the womb. These, monks, are the four ways of entering the womb. : : : The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four types of persons (*pudgala*). What four? Here, monks, one person dwells having attained the destruction of the taints (*āsravakṣaya*) in this very life, through his own higher knowledge, having realized it for himself with direct experience, and abiding therein. This, monks, is the first type of person. Furthermore, monks, one person dwells having attained the destruction of the taints in this very life, through his own higher knowledge, having realized it for himself with direct experience, and abiding therein;

furthermore, he possesses the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and is skilled in the various modes of eloquence. This, monks, is the second type of person. Furthermore, monks, one person dwells having attained the destruction of the taints in this very life, through his own higher knowledge, having realized it for himself with direct experience, and abiding therein; furthermore, he possesses the analytical knowledges, is skilled in the various modes of eloquence, and is a teacher of the Dharma who delights in teaching the Dharma to others. This, monks, is the third type of person. Furthermore, monks, one person dwells having attained the destruction of the taints in this very life, through his own higher knowledge, having realized it for himself with direct experience, and abiding therein; furthermore, he possesses the analytical knowledges, is skilled in the various modes of eloquence, is a teacher of the Dharma who delights in teaching the Dharma to others, and is one who has reached the ultimate limit of the holy life. This, monks, is the fourth type of person. These, monks, are the four types of persons. : : : The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four fruits of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*). What four? The fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*), the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), and the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala*). These, monks, are the four fruits of the ascetic life. : : : The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*). What four? Here, monks, a noble disciple is content with whatever robe he obtains, saying: ‘This is sufficient for me to ward off the cold, to ward off the heat, to ward off the touch of flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and serpents. He is content with whatever almsfood he obtains, saying: ‘This is sufficient for me to maintain this body and to prevent its harm, so that I may dwell in comfort and without hindrance. He is content with whatever lodging he obtains, saying: ‘This is sufficient for me to ward off the heat, to ward off the cold, to ward off the touch of flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and serpents. He delights in the abandonment of the world, delights in the solitude of seclusion, and finds joy in the practice of meditation. These, monks, are the four noble lineages. : : : The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). What four? The basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of desire and volitional effort of striving; the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of energy and volitional effort of striving; the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of mind and volitional effort of striving; and the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of investigation and volitional effort of striving. These, monks, are the four bases of psychic power. : : : The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four establishments of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). What four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... He dwells contemplating mind in the mind... He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. These, monks, are the four establishments of mindfulness. : : : The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four right endeavors (*samyakprahāṇa*). What four? Here, monks, a monk generates desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states; he makes an effort, applies energy, exerts his mind, and strives. He generates desire for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states; he makes an effort, applies energy, exerts his mind, and strives. He generates desire for the arising of unarisen wholesome states; he makes an effort, applies energy, exerts his mind, and strives. He generates desire for the maintenance, non-decline, increase, expansion, fulfillment, and completion of arisen wholesome states; he makes an effort, applies energy, exerts his mind, and strives. These, monks, are the four right endeavors. : : : The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). What four? The basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of desire and volitional effort of striving; the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of energy and volitional effort of striving; the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of mind and volitional effort of striving; and the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of investigation and volitional effort of striving. These, monks, are the four bases of psychic power. : : : The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four noble truths (*āryasatya*). What four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. These, monks, are the four noble truths. : : : The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four fruits of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*). What four? The fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship. These, monks, are the four fruits of the ascetic life. : : : The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*). What four? Here, monks, a noble disciple is content with whatever robe he obtains, saying: ‘This is sufficient for me to ward off the cold, to ward off the heat, to ward off the touch of flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and serpents. He is content with whatever almsfood he obtains, saying: ‘This is sufficient for me to maintain this body and to prevent its harm, so that I may dwell in comfort and without hindrance. He is content with whatever lodging he obtains, saying: ‘This is sufficient for me to ward off the heat, to ward off the cold, to ward off the touch of flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and serpents. He delights in the abandonment of the world, delights in the solitude of seclusion, and finds joy in the practice of meditation. These, monks, are the four noble lineages. : : : The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four right endeavors (*samyakprahāṇa*). What four? Here, monks, a monk generates desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states; he makes an effort, applies energy, exerts his mind, and strives. He generates desire for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states; he makes an effort, applies energy, exerts his mind, and strives. He generates desire for the arising of unarisen wholesome states; he makes an effort, applies energy, exerts his mind, and strives. He generates desire for the maintenance, non-decline, increase, expansion, fulfillment, and completion of arisen wholesome states; he makes an effort, applies energy, exerts his mind, and strives. These, monks, are the four right endeavors. : : :

[The verse continues: "Just as a man who has fallen into a pit of excrement, having been pulled out by others, would not wish to enter it again; so too, one who has seen the danger of the world does not desire to return to existence. [The commentary states: "Just as a man who has fallen into a pit of excrement and been pulled out by others would not wish to enter that same pit again, even though he might be offered great wealth; in the same way, one who has seen the peril of cyclic existence through the wisdom of discernment does not desire to return to existence, even if offered the sovereignty over the three realms. Therefore, it is said: 'One who has seen the danger of the world does not desire to return to existence. [The verse continues: "Just as a man who has been struck by a poisoned arrow, though his wound is dressed with medicine, does not find peace until he has extracted the arrow; so too, one who has seen the danger of the world does not find peace until he has abandoned all attachments. [The commentary states: "Just as a man who has been struck by a poisoned arrow, though his wound is treated with medicinal ointments and bandages, does not find relief until the arrow itself has been removed; in the same way, one who has seen the peril of cyclic existence does not find peace until all forms of attachment have been completely abandoned. Therefore, it is said: 'One who has seen the danger of the world does not find peace until he has abandoned all attachments. [The verse continues: "Just as a man who has escaped from a burning house, having seen its many perils, does not wish to enter it again even for the sake of his life; so too, one who has seen the danger of the world does not wish to return to existence. [The commentary states: "Just as a man who has escaped from a burning house, having clearly perceived its various dangers such as fire and smoke, does not wish to enter that house again even at the cost of his own life; in the same way, one who has seen the peril of cyclic existence does not wish to return to existence. Therefore, it is said: 'One who has seen the danger of the world does not wish to return to existence. Therefore, it is said: 'One who has seen the danger of the world does not wish to return to existence. [The commentary states: "Just as a man who has been freed from a chronic, debilitating illness after enduring its long-term suffering, does not wish to contract that disease again even at the cost of his life; in the same way, one who has seen the peril of cyclic existence does not wish to return to existence. Therefore, it is said: 'One who has seen the danger of the world does not wish to return to existence. Therefore, it is said: 'One who has seen the danger of the world does not wish to return to existence. Therefore, it is said: 'One who has seen the danger of the world does not wish to return to existence. [The commentary states: "Just as a man who has been liberated from the dominion of a tyrannical king, having experienced its various afflictions and hardships, does not wish to submit to that king's power again even for the sake of his physical well-being; in the same way, one who has seen the peril of cyclic existence does not wish to return to existence. Therefore, it is said: 'One who has seen the danger of the world does not wish to return to existence. [The commentary states: "Just as a man who has been freed from the grasp of a malevolent spirit or demon, having endured its various fears, does not wish to be possessed by that demon again even at the cost of his life; in the same way, one who has seen the peril of cyclic existence does not wish to return to existence. R44: The Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path. The Blessed One said: "Monks, these four noble truths are to be realized by direct knowledge. What four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. These four noble truths were taught by the Blessed One as they truly are. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall fully understand the noble truth of suffering through direct knowledge; we shall abandon the noble truth of the origin of suffering through direct knowledge; we shall realize the noble truth of the cessation of suffering through direct knowledge; we shall cultivate the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering through direct knowledge. This is how you should train yourselves. R44: The Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path. Monks, for one who has not seen these four noble truths as they truly are, there is no transcending of birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; there is no transcending of suffering, I say. Monks, for one who has seen these four noble truths as they truly are, there is the transcending of birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; there is the transcending of suffering, I say. What four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Monks, what is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering; aging is suffering; illness is suffering; death is suffering; association with the disliked is suffering; separation from the liked is suffering; not to obtain what one desires is suffering; in brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering. This, monks, is called the noble truth of suffering. Monks, what is the noble truth of the origin of suffering? It is this craving which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there; namely, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. This, monks, is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering. Monks, what is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering? It is the complete fading away and cessation of that same craving, giving it up, relinquishing it, letting go of it, and not relying on it. This, monks, is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. Monks, what is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering? It is this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, monks, is called the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. R44: The Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path. The Blessed One said this: "Monks, there are these four ways of undertaking things. What four? There is a way of undertaking things that is painful with sluggish result; there is a way of undertaking things that is painful with swift result; there is a way of undertaking things that is pleasant with sluggish result; and there is a way of undertaking things that is pleasant with swift result. And what, monks, is the way of undertaking things that is painful with sluggish result?

Here, monks, someone undertakes a bodily action that is painful, and undertakes a verbal action that is painful, and undertakes a mental action that is painful; and he is not endowed with faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom. This, monks, is called the way of undertaking things that is painful with sluggish result. And what, monks, is the way of undertaking things that is painful with swift result? Here, monks, someone undertakes a bodily action that is painful, and undertakes a verbal action that is painful, and undertakes a mental action that is painful; yet he is endowed with faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom. This, monks, is called the way of undertaking things that is painful with swift result. And what, monks, is the way of undertaking things that is pleasant with sluggish result? Here, monks, someone undertakes a bodily action that is pleasant, and undertakes a verbal action that is pleasant, and undertakes a mental action that is pleasant; yet he is not endowed with faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom. This, monks, is called the way of undertaking things that is pleasant with sluggish result. And what, monks, is the way of undertaking things that is pleasant with swift result? Here, monks, someone undertakes a bodily action that is pleasant, and undertakes a verbal action that is pleasant, and undertakes a mental action that is pleasant; and he is endowed with faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom. This, monks, is called the way of undertaking things that is pleasant with swift result. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having thus spoken, the Well-Farer, the Teacher, further said this: "Painful with sluggish result, Painful with swift result, Pleasant with sluggish result, Pleasant with swift result— These are the four ways of undertaking things That have been taught by the Buddha."

The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, this Dharma discourse is named ‘The Array of the Qualities of the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Amitābha. You should remember it by this name. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a lotus flower; the person who is like a blue lotus flower; the person who is like a white lotus flower; and the person who is like a fragrant lotus flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind overcome by sensual lust, burning with sensual lust, and he does not attain the destruction of the taints in this very life. But when he is separated from that body after death, he is reborn in a company of devas of the sense-sphere. There, too, he dwells with his mind overcome by sensual lust, burning with sensual lust, and he does not attain the destruction of the taints in that state. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four?

The person who is like a lotus flower growing in the mud of a pond, yet remains unstained by that mud; the person who is like a lotus flower growing in the mud of a pond, yet is only half-developed; the person who is like a lotus flower growing in the mud of a pond, yet has not yet emerged from the water; and the person who is like a lotus flower growing in the mud of a pond, yet has emerged from the water and stands above it, unstained by the water.
These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”

The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence.

The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? “Monks, here, some person is one who dwells having attained the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya) in this very life, having realized it for himself with direct knowledge, and abiding therein; he has understood: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being. This is called the first kind of person found existing in the world. “Furthermore, monks, some person is one who, with the utter destruction of the five lower fetters (orambhāgiya-saṃyojana), has become a non-returner (anāgāmī); he will attain parinirvāṇa there, not returning from that world. This is called the second kind of person found existing in the world. “Furthermore, monks, some person is one who, with the utter destruction of three fetters and with the attenuation of greed, hatred, and delusion, has become a once-returner (sakadāgāmī); having returned only once more to this human world, he will put an end to suffering. This is called the third kind of person found existing in the world. “Furthermore, monks, some person is one who, with the utter destruction of the three fetters, has become a stream-enterer (sotāpanna), no longer subject to perdition, fixed in destiny, and assured of enlightenment. This is called the fourth kind of person found existing in the world. “These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. : : : Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said: “It is wonderful, venerable sir, it is marvelous how well the Blessed One has taught the Dhamma by way of types of persons! Suppose, venerable sir, there were a great mountain range extending for a hundred yojanas, two hundred yojanas, three hundred yojanas, or even four hundred yojanas, composed entirely of solid rock, without any clefts or fissures. A man might come along bringing a wisp of cotton wool or a tuft of cotton. He might think: ‘I shall pierce this great mountain range with this wisp of cotton wool or tuft of cotton. What do you think, Ānanda, would that man be able to pierce that great mountain range with that wisp of cotton wool or tuft of cotton? “Certainly not, venerable sir. Why is that? Because that great mountain range is so vast, so solid, and so firm. “It is just so, Ānanda. These four kinds of persons have been declared by me to be those who have reached the goal, accomplished their task, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained their own goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and are liberated through final knowledge. Yet, Ānanda, there are other beings who, having heard this Dhamma, develop it in such a way that they too reach the goal, accomplish their task, do what was to be done, lay down the burden, attain their own goal, destroy the fetters of existence, and are liberated through final knowledge. Therefore, Ānanda, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall hear the Dhamma from the Teacher or from one who has heard it from the Teacher, and we shall develop it in such a way that we too reach the goal, accomplish our task, do what was to be done, lay down the burden, attain our own goal, destroy the fetters of existence, and are liberated through final knowledge. It is in this way, Ānanda, that you should train yourselves. : : : At Sāvatthī. 377 63. da: "Then" (tataḥ) means "thereafter. It indicates that immediately following the previous [verse], one should practice as follows. Regarding this, it is taught in the *Guhyasamāja-tantra*: "One who desires to accomplish all mantras should always practice the yoga of the three mandalas. Furthermore, it is stated in the *Vajraśekhara-tantra*: "The yogin should always practice the yoga of the three mandalas. This refers to the yoga of the three mandalas consisting of the body, speech, and mind. As for the method of practicing that yoga, it is taught in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*: "Having entered the supreme mandala, one should visualize the three mandalas within the body; then, having visualized the three mandalas, one should perform the recitation. This means that after entering the supreme mandala, one should visualize the three mandalas within the body, and subsequently, having visualized the three mandalas, one should perform the recitation. Regarding the visualization of the three mandalas within the body, it is taught in the *Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha*: "One should visualize the body-mandala, the speech-mandala, and the mind-mandala; these three mandalas should be visualized within the body. This means that one should visualize the body-mandala, the speech-mandala, and the mind-mandala, and these three mandalas should be visualized within the body. Regarding the performance of the recitation after visualizing the three mandalas, it is taught in the *Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha*: "Having visualized the three mandalas, one should perform the recitation; one should recite with the mantra of the three mandalas. This means that after visualizing the three mandalas, one should perform the recitation, and one should recite using the mantra of the three mandalas. Regarding the mantra of the three mandalas, it is taught in the *Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha*: "OṂ VAJRA-SATVA HŪṂ; OṂ VAJRA-RATNA TRĀṂ; OṂ VAJRA-DHARMA HRĪḤ; OṂ VAJRA-KARMA ĀḤ. These are the four mantras of the four families. Among these, the first, OṂ VAJRA-SATVA HŪṂ, is the mantra of the Tathāgata family. The second, OṂ VAJRA-RATNA TRĀṂ, is the mantra of the Jewel family. The third, OṂ VAJRA-DHARMA HRĪḤ, is the mantra of the Lotus family. The fourth, OṂ VAJRA-KARMA ĀḤ, is the mantra of the Action family. One should recite these four mantras according to the sequence of the four families. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a lotus flower; the person who is like a blue lotus flower; the person who is like a white lotus flower; and the person who is like a fragrant lotus flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind overcome by sensual lust, burning with sensual lust, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen sensual lust. Yet he does not give rise to the thought: ‘My mind dwells with sensual lust, it burns with sensual lust, and I do not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen sensual lust. He does not disclose his fault to the Teacher or to wise companions in the holy life. This, monks, is called a person like a lotus flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a blue lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind overcome by ill will, burning with ill will, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen ill will. Yet he does not give rise to the thought: ‘My mind dwells with ill will, it burns with ill will, and I do not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen ill will. He does not disclose his fault to the Teacher or to wise companions in the holy life. This, monks, is called a person like a blue lotus flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a white lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind overcome by sloth and torpor, burning with sloth and torpor, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen sloth and torpor. Yet he does not give rise to the thought: ‘My mind dwells with sloth and torpor, it burns with sloth and torpor, and I do not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen sloth and torpor.

He does not disclose his fault to the Teacher or to wise companions in the holy life. This, monks, is called a person like a white lotus flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a fragrant lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind overcome by doubt, burning with doubt, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen doubt. Yet he does not give rise to the thought: ‘My mind dwells with doubt, it burns with doubt, and I do not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen doubt. He does not disclose his fault to the Teacher or to wise companions in the holy life. This, monks, is called a person like a fragrant lotus flower. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. : : :

1385 288: The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a self, nor does he perceive a sentient being, a soul, or a person. He does not perceive form, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. He does not perceive the eye, nor does he perceive forms, nor does he perceive eye-consciousness. He does not perceive the ear, nor does he perceive sounds, nor does he perceive ear-consciousness.

He does not perceive the nose, nor does he perceive odors, nor does he perceive nose-consciousness. He does not perceive the tongue, nor does he perceive tastes, nor does he perceive tongue-consciousness. He does not perceive the body, nor does he perceive tangibles, nor does he perceive body-consciousness. He does not perceive the mind, nor does he perceive mental phenomena, nor does he perceive mind-consciousness. He does not perceive the element of earth, nor does he perceive the element of water, nor does he perceive the element of fire, nor does he perceive the element of wind, nor does he perceive the element of space, nor does he perceive the element of consciousness. He does not perceive the realm of desire, nor does he perceive the realm of form, nor does he perceive the formless realm. He does not perceive conditioned phenomena, nor does he perceive unconditioned phenomena. He does not perceive the past, nor does he perceive the future, nor does he perceive the present. Subhūti, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive anything that he is called a 'bodhisattva. Why is that? Subhūti, it is because there is no dharma whatsoever that can be apprehended as a 'bodhisattva,' nor is there any dharma that can be apprehended as 'perfection of wisdom. Since these two dharmas cannot be apprehended, they are neither conjoined nor disjoined, and they are neither distinct nor non-distinct. Therefore, Subhūti, this is called the 'perfection of wisdom' of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Then the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to train in the perfection of wisdom train? The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to train in the perfection of wisdom should train in the same way that space trains. Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to train in the perfection of wisdom should train in the same way that all dharmas are unarisen and unceasing. Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to train in the perfection of wisdom should train in the same way that all dharmas are empty and signless. Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to train in the perfection of wisdom should train in the same way that all dharmas are wishless and beyond conceptualization. Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to train in the perfection of wisdom should train in the same way that all dharmas are like an illusion, like a dream, like a mirage, like an echo, like a reflection, like a city of gandharvas, and like a magical creation. Know, O child, that the entire world, the three realms with all things moving and unmoving, arises from the gods; know that the supreme reality is the truth, and that the ancestors are the sons of the sages.

In this regard, it must be explained that the direct birth of the Pitṛs from the body of Brahmā seen in the Purāṇas refers to Marīci and others in their capacity as Pitṛs, whereas the birth from the body of Brahmā through an intermediary refers to them in their capacity as the fathers of Marīci and the others; thus, there is no contradiction with the Śruti.

And thus, it is understood that those who are the sons of Marīci and the others are the *pitaraḥ* (fathers), Marīci and the others are the *pitāmahāḥ* (grandfathers), and Brahmā is the *prapitāmahaḥ* (great-grandfather). That which is Brahmā is the mantra denoted by the word "Prati," the great-grandfather. And Marīci and the others are the seasons (*ṛtavaḥ*), the grandfathers; and the months are the seasonal periods (*ārtavāḥ*).
There is no contradiction among the Purāṇas regarding the term "Pitṛs":

Thus, according to the statement of Manu, even the birth of Yama, Marīci, and others from the body of Brahmā is justified by the difference in kalpas and the resulting difference in creation. Now, as for these ancestors (pitṛs),

This is because it is seen in Pāraskara’s extension (*atideśa*) that "the horn [is used] as in the *vṛddhi* [rite]"; for extensions occur when there is a difference [between rites].

Regarding the *viṣṭi* [lunar days], the *mṛtyus*, and the *kabhīṅga* śrāddhas, when there is the thought of obtaining new grain (*navānnalābha*), here too the procedure for the śrāddha will be stated in the section on the food for śrāddhas, beginning with "rice, barley, and millet," etc. However, the author of the *Smṛticandrikā* considers it to be [a matter] regarding the new moon day (*navānnabhaṃ mati*).

He states that when a father performs a *śrāddha* with new grain before the time for eating new grain has arrived, the two deities of the *vaiśvadevika* rite— namely Hī and Kālakāmī— are to be invoked as the presiding divinities.
Furthermore, this applies to those *vaiśvadevika* rites performed under the authority of a specific occasion (*nimitta-adhikāra*).

The phrase "when the sun has entered Virgo" (kanyāgata-gardā) serves as an illustration for the *gādi* śrāddhas; this refers to the second fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, and it is intended for the purpose of introducing the optional (*kāmya*) śrāddhas.

Thus, because of the contradiction [otherwise] and based on the scriptural statement, it is established that by the term "occasional" (*naimittika*), a śrāddha performed on occasions such as the acquisition of new grain is meant.

Regarding the statement, "In the case of the *naimittika* [rite], there is freedom regarding time (*kāla*) and desire (*kāma*)," the word *naimittika* here refers to the *piṇḍīkaraṇa* rite performed on the eleventh day (*ekādaśāha*). Consequently, because that [rite] contains the two primary forms— namely, the *ekoddiṣṭa* and the *pārvaṇa*— and includes the *śrāddha* for the gods (*daivika*), it is said that there is freedom regarding time and desire therein.
It is joined with the source (yonidhi). Again, for the mother, it is like the blowing of a conch shell. Some desire one *koḍi* per year.
However, that which is performed in place of the *koḍi* called by the term "occasional" (*naimittika*) is also an occasional rite (*naimittika*), even though it is a daily offering (*tadāhnika*).

The procedure for the desire for time (*kālakāma*) regarding those [offerings] is brief. Therefore, even when two names are employed, only the plural form should be used, and not the dual.
Its intention must be understood as follows: as for the reason stated here by the author of the *Smṛticandrikā* regarding the use of the plural number— namely,

that it is "in order to exclude the three [other] Āndhras," based on the observation of the use of plural endings in many *smṛtis* and *purāṇas* when asking [the question]— "let that be so" in the case of that which stands in the place of a mantra.

Because each individual *preṣa* (prompting) occurs as a separate application, this statement was made with reference to the *preṣa*-sentences themselves; for otherwise, such an intention would be impossible. As for the argument that it is based on the observation of the use of plural forms—such as "having grasped [the cup] without the thumb, they summon the Viśve Devās"—that is not a valid application.

Even by means of the *viśvadevānumantraṇa* mantra addressed to Vāyu, the plural number in the injunctive statement is indeed justified. Furthermore, because of such statements as, "When the performance of the *piṇḍa* has been completed for him according to the Dharma, the completion of the *piṇḍa* should be performed by the liberated ones through this very state," and because the mere offering of the *piṇḍa* is prescribed when the feeding of Brahmins is impossible, thus, from these observed indications, the primacy of the *piṇḍa*-offering is understood; therefore, of this alone—

The word *śrāddha* is a name [for the rite]. Now, one might argue that even the feeding of the Brāhmaṇas possesses primacy here because of its connection with the principal deities in the form of the ancestors (*pitṛs*). This is not so; for the feeding [itself] is directly connected to the Brāhmaṇas by virtue of the scriptural statement, "If one should feed even a single person at a *śrāddha*," and by the inherent capacity of the act of feeding itself.

Because there is no authoritative evidence for [the word *pitrya*] referring to the ancestors (*pitaras*). [Objection: If that were so, then, like the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, the designation *pitrya* would be a mere figurative usage (*upacāra*). [Reply: No, because that is possible due to its being for the sake of the *śrāddha* and for the sake of the Brahmins. [Objection: Is it not the case that the meaning of the word *śrāddha* is merely the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), since one says, "He has eaten the *śrāddha*" even when [the food] is placed in the vessel for the rice-balls?

How is the application [of the term] to be understood? We say it is by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), referring to that which is the act of frying as an auxiliary part of the ancestral rite (*śrāddha*). Therefore, the name "piṇḍadāna" (offering of rice-balls) applies here. Thus, in certain applications where the offering of rice-balls has not been accomplished, the intention arises regarding the application; furthermore, the rice-balls are the vessels for the Brahmins.

The function of the ancillaries (*aṅga*) is for the sake of the primary element (*pradhāna*). For instance, the feeding of Brāhmaṇas and so forth are ancillaries to that gift. Others say: "The feeding of Brāhmaṇas alone is the primary element; it is precisely there that the designation 'Śrāddha' applies. Thus says the Āpastamba-sūtra: "Prajāpati proclaimed this rite by the name 'Śrāddha'..."

In that context, for the sake of spiritual welfare (*śreya*), the ancestors are deities; this is for the purpose of protecting the status of the Brāhmaṇas. Regarding the *āhavanīya* fire, a distinct function (*kārya*) exists for that which is being offered into the *āhavanīya*. And since those [ancestors] are not eating, they are unable to perform that function; therefore, by implication, [the rite] must extend as far as the feeding of the Brāhmaṇas.
This is the rule for the speech [of the teacher]. Therefore Yājñavalkya said:
"Then one may speak as one pleases; they too [the students] are restrained in speech."

Thus, in this way, [there is] the activity of the instigator (prayojaka-vyāpāra) which has as its object the activity of the one being instigated (prayojya-vyāpāra), consisting in the feeding of the Brahmins.

The section on the *śrāddha* (ancestral rite) consists of fifteen chapters, because it extends up to the attainment of the *gārhapatya* and *āhavanīya* fires; for the *śrāddha* is designated as a *homa* (oblation).
Because it reaches as far as the acquisition of the *gārhapatya* and *āhavanīya* fires, the *śrāddha* is understood as being designated as a *homa*.

Thus, the word *śrāddha* is the name for the instigating activity of the sacrificer known as the feeding of Brahmins. As for the view of Viśvarūpa and others, which was introduced by way of refutation— that because the activity of the person being prompted (the *prayojya*) is inseparable from the activity of the prompter (*prayojaka*), the [action] has the Brahmin as its agent— [that is incorrect].

Even the act of eating, which consists of the operation of the one being employed, is denoted by the word *śrāddha*. For this very reason, we observe the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the word *śrāddha* with the verb "to eat," as in the expression, "He eats the *śrāddha*. Likewise, there are such indications as, "Whichever of these he eats, having honored the *śrāddha*," and so forth. Furthermore:

In a *śrāddha* performed while the father is still living, since there is no offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) by those who are alive, the injunction regarding the meal (*bhojana-vidhāna*) indicates the primacy of the vessel and the activities conducive to it. Thus, it says: "Or he should cause his own father to eat like a Brahmin," and "Or his grandfather should eat that *śrāddha*," and so forth.

This appears to me to be incorrect; for since the operation of the person to be employed (*prayojya*) is not the operation of the qualified agent (*adhikārin*), it lacks a connection with the fruit, and because its status as the primary [action] is untenable, how could there be a designation of the primary agent? it is stated that [the rite] is designated by the term *yāka-śrāddha*. Now, if this is so, then [what of] the activities of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) such as the *Āgneya* and other [sacrifices]?

In the absence of primacy (*pradhānatva*), there would be no designation by the terms *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa*. Even though that which is enjoined as the activity of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is accomplished through the activity of the priests (*ṛtvij*) performed by another person, it is nonetheless accomplished by the activity consisting of the sacrificer’s own mental resolve (*bhāvanā*); therefore, it is primary.

There is no contradiction in the fact that the terms *darśapūrṇamāsa* denote that which brings about prosperity (*śrī*). However, since eating— which is accomplished through the activity of the non-sacrificer—
is designated as the activity of the sacrificer,

it does not fall under the denotation of the term *śrāddha*, even though it is pervaded by the sacrificer’s efficient force (*bhāvanā*), just as in the case of the injunction regarding the efficient force of giving.

Because acceptance (*pratigraha*) is the pervading factor (*vyāpaka*), even though it is included within the mental disposition (*bhāvanā*), it is not denoted by the word "giving" (*dāna*). For here too, the meaning of the word "giving" is the production of another's ownership preceded by the cessation of one's own [ownership]. The production of another's ownership is not accomplished without bringing about acceptance; for it is through acceptance that another's ownership is brought to completion.

Therefore, even in the case of receiving a gift (*pratigraha*), there certainly exists the state of being pervaded by the cultivation of giving (*dānabhāvanā*). However, because it lacks an injunction (*vidhi*) as an activity of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), it is not primary. This is because an injunction of the sacrificer is impossible in the act of receiving;
for according to the established principle, a person is enjoined as an agent only with respect to their own activity. Nor is [the sacrificer] [enjoined] in the act of receiving...

The meaning of this is as follows: it is not our view that its parts are inherent (*svābhāvika*), because this [entity] is eternal, whereas parts belong only to what is non-eternal. For that which is called "having parts" (*sāvayava*) is subject to disintegration. Furthermore, that which is distinct from destruction is necessarily subject to destruction. Now, one might object: a "part" is merely that which inheres in parts, but this [entity] is not such.

Do not say so; for it would follow that even the universal (*sāmānya*) possesses parts. Furthermore, one must state whether the parts of the whole are themselves wholes or possess a different dimension than the whole. In the former case, its omnipresence (*vibhutva*) and oneness (*ekatva*) would be lost. In the latter case, there would be no distinction from [other] entities such as atoms (*paramāṇu*).

And it is well known from the *Smṛtis*, *Purāṇas*, and other sources. One might think that its parts are innate; nevertheless, he says "born of causes" (*hetujāḥ*) to show that they can also be adventitious (*aupādhika*).
These [parts] are the morning, midday, afternoon, day, night, fortnight, month, season, and year.

Furthermore, [these] consist of divisions characterized by the creation and so forth of those [worlds], which are specific modifications of the solar motion; they are born from that, being dependent upon its limitation. Thus, they are manifold according to the distinctions of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya) rituals. The meaning of this is as follows: That specific deity named Prajāpati who is heard of in the scriptures is none other than this very time consisting of the year. This [year] has two parts. Among these, the northern solstice (*udagayana*), Śakra, day, and forenoon constitute one part; [the other is] the northern solstice, which is the portion of the sun being traversed starting from Capricorn (*makara*).

Time is characterized by the six signs of the zodiac (*rāśi*). The bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) is the period beginning from the first lunar day (*pratipad*) following the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) until the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*).
A day (*ahar*) is the daytime. The forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) is the first division of that [day]. Thus it is stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:

"From the turning point [of the shadow] until the forenoon, and from that until the afternoon"—thus it was said regarding the shadow. The time delimited by the turning of the shadow is the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*). This entire collection of divisions of the year belongs to the gods; herein, O Goddess—

The meaning is: what actions are to be performed? The second part consists of the *dakṣiṇāyana* (the sun’s southern course) and *tāmisra* (the night). *Dakṣiṇāyana* refers to the period of time characterized by the six zodiac signs beginning with Cancer, which are traversed by the sun. *Tāmisra* refers to the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), beginning from the full moon day up to the first day (*pratipad*) of the lunar month.

The period ending with the new moon (amāvāsyā) is [the time for the ancestors]. The period delimited by the non-appearance of the sun, separated from Mount Meru, is [the time for the gods]. This entire collection of divisions of the year belongs to the Pitṛs; the meaning is that the ancestral rites (pitrya-karma) should be performed therein.
Thus, time is twofold—by way of being divine and by way of being ancestral—and there is no other state.

The state of having the nature of both [gods and ancestors]. Why? Because there is no other time. Since there is no time remaining beyond the year, all time is exactly that much. In rites such as the *vṛddhiśrāddha*, the time begins at dawn and so forth. Some maintain that it belongs to the time of the cow, while others say it occurs before the first drop of milk.

In this context, although the injunction regarding the midday [fire-laying] immediately following the statement "Therefore, one should indeed lay [the fires] at midday" establishes the connection between the fire-laying and the *āsvayana* sacrifice, the fivefold division is heard as a subordinate element (*śeṣa*).

Being subsisted upon by those who have performed their duties, it attains a connection with all desires. For this very reason, this division into five parts, consisting of components of immeasurable magnitude, is seen as being entirely common to all.

And so it is stated in the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*: "The morning consists of three muhūrtas, and the forenoon (*māṅgava*) is of the same duration; midday should consist of three muhūrtas, and the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) is likewise."
Then, at the end of three muhūrtas, [the world] was rendered entirely armored by Māyā.

Then there are three muhūrtas called Maṅgalya, followed by midday (madhyāhna);

whatever is prescribed among these [times], that a wise person should perform.

The "line" (*rekhā*) is that portion of the rising solar disc which shines like a streak and is fit for its first perception; it is "from the sun" (*ādityāt*), meaning from the sunrise. It is so stated; for it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa:

The meaning is that whatever rite is prescribed for these specific times, such as the morning and so forth, one should perform each of those during these respective periods measured by three *muhūrtas*.

Even though there exists a conventional designation (*saṃjñā*) for the first six *muhūrta*s of the day consisting of "morning" (*prātaḥ*) and "forenoon" (*saṅgava*), nevertheless—

when the day is divided into two parts, the period from the middle moment until its end is midday, which is sufficient for the performance of the various prescribed rites. And here, one should not admit the application of any contradictory alternative designation.

from the beginning of the second quarter of the twelfth muhūrta until sunset. There is a fivefold division: from the thirteenth muhūrta until sunset is called the day.

Regarding this, some maintain that the interval [of time] is established by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), while others hold it to be the cessation of the period measured by the *pūrva* [period]. Alternatively, it serves to exclude other regions.

Furthermore, it must be stated that its meaningfulness (*arthavattva*) consists in its being intended to establish the excellence (*prāśastya*) of its own subject matter. In this regard, on the first alternative, there would be both the futility (*ānarthakya*) and the sublation (*bādha*) of the statement regarding the major period (*mahāvadhi*). Therefore, it is determined that the statement regarding the intermediate period (*avāntarāvadhi*) is for the purpose of indicating a state of being more excellent.
In the Skanda and Vāyu Purāṇas: Now, regarding the Kutapaka [time]:
"Where the Lord of Rays (the Sun) intensely heats the earth with his rays."
The Kutapa period is not the time [for this]; that which is given there yields great fruit.
The word ‘ku’ refers to the earth; ‘gopatiḥ’ (the lord of rays) is the sun; that moment in which he ‘tapatī’ (shines), making it hot with his own ‘gobhiḥ’ (rays), is that time.

*Kutapa* means victory (*jaya*). By this, the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of the word *kutapa* has been established, and it has been defined as such. For when the sun is at the very center of the earth—due to the contraction of the shadow of all beings—it heats the entire earth; thus, being at the center of the day, it is designated as *kutapa*.
Even that which is measured by a *muhūrta* is designated by the word "moment" (*kṣaṇa*) through a figurative usage based on its own nature;
for it is stated thus in the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
The Kutapa period is to be known as beginning from the eighth muhūrta after midday and ending before the ninth;
that which is given to the ancestors during this time becomes inexhaustible.
In the *Prabhāmaṇḍala* it is also said:
"There are fifteen well-known *muhūrtas*;
among them, the eighth *muhūrta* is known as the time called *kutapa*."

As for items such as the sword and the bowl, however, because they are situated within the scope of the term *kutapa* at midday, they cannot be separated [from it]; thus, they are mentioned by way of association with midday.

It is said in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:

however, because of the departure [of the ancestors] during the dark fortnight, he should not let the Rohiṇī [nakṣatra] pass by."

If the *kutapa* [time] falls within the first half of the day during the bright fortnight (*pūrṇapakṣa*), the commencement of the *śrāddha* should take place either in the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) or at the *parvaṇa* [junction]. However, in the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), it should occur only in the second half of the *kutapa*.
[5.0] This statement is intended to establish that in the *pārvaṇa* rite, the first half of the *kutapa* period is to be adopted, whereas in the *ekoddiṣṭa*, the second half is to be adopted.
For, by way of reversal, the rule for the forenoon and afternoon of the two halves [of the month] is already established through other injunctions regarding midday meals and non-meals.

Alternatively, by the phrase "of the bright fortnight," the *daivika* (divine) *śrāddha* prescribed for that fortnight is indicated, and the forenoon is ordained; by the phrase "of the dark fortnight," the *paitṛka* (ancestral) is indicated, and the afternoon is ordained.

And thus, by not contradicting other specific [scriptural] injunctions, the two times—the midday and the afternoon—will not be sublated when they fall within the [general] period for the *mṛtāṅga* rite. Among these, the application of the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) is first analyzed. Śātātapa says:
That which is proclaimed as the *darśa-śrāddha* is indeed declared to be the *pārvaṇa*;
and that gift to the ancestors in the afternoon is highly praised.

Regarding the Darśa-śrāddha, which is performed without the Piṇḍapitṛyajña or is performed by those who do not maintain the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), the Kalpasūtra author states: "In the afternoon, they perform the Piṇḍapitṛyajña.
Thus, it is prescribed that this occurs after the Piṇḍapitṛyajña at the end of the afternoon.
Therefore, one should take as much as is available of the nectar portion divided by the knowledge-measure; thus it is said here:
"By that [measure]."
Likewise:
"The Śrāddha consisting of the Piṇḍānvāhāryaka is performed when the moon has set;
it should not be done at dawn, nor too close to the evening twilight."
On the new moon day, a learned Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires should perform the Piṇḍānvāhāryaka Śrāddha every month for his beloved ancestors.

And this need not be said: that the *Anvāhāryaka* Śrāddha must follow immediately after the *Tarpaṇa* sacrifice—which is included among the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*)—because of the statement in the *Matsya Purāṇa*: "He who possesses the sacred fire should always perform the *Pitṛyajña* known as *Tarpaṇa*, and then perform the *Anvāhāryaka* Śrāddha for the satisfaction of the ancestors. Thus, the *Anvāhāryaka* does not necessarily follow the *Tarpaṇa*.
In the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, in the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* [Section 50],
it is stated that [the rite] follows immediately after the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*. Accordingly, the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) is to be understood as the time for its performance.
As Logākṣi has said:
"Having completed the *pañcānta* rite, the wise householder should perform the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice; thereafter, he should perform the *piṇḍayajña*, and after that, the *āgrahāyaṇī*."
Therefore, for the Darśa-śrāddha, which is to be performed after the Piṇḍapitṛyajña,
the third part of the day— extending up to the proximity of the evening twilight— is prescribed as the time for its completion.
It is to be grasped.
Thus ends the application for the later time. Now follows the application for the earlier time.
In that context, regarding the statement "the *daivika* śrāddha is in the forenoon," since there is no cooked food (*pakva*) in the *pīla* which constitutes a limb of the *daivika* śrāddha,
this is stated with reference to the *āmāśrāddha* (uncooked-food śrāddha) which is its constituent part. In that regard,
the rule "the *āmāśrāddha* is in the forenoon" refers exclusively to the *āmāśrāddha* performed by twice-born men (*dvija*), and not to the *āmāśrāddha* performed by others.

Some have determined that it is also the subject matter (*viṣaya*). For he thinks: if both were the subject matter of a desire for performance by the agent, then—having effected an absolute sublation of what was obtained from the other in one case—it would be established as optional in the other; thus, a disparity would arise where there is permanence in one case and optionality in the other.
For instance:
in the case of the *śrāddha* for twice-born ancestors, one should set aside the afternoon time (*aparāhṇa*)— which is obtained by extension (*atideśika*)—
and establish the morning time (*pūrva*), because the direct instruction (*upadeśa*) "let there be the morning [time]" is stronger than the extended rule (*atideśa*).

One should not establish that the *upadeśika* [injunction] of the afternoon (*aparāhna*) has only an optional (*pākṣika*) sublation, because it is equal in strength to another *upadeśa* regarding the *śūdrāmantra*. Therefore, one should establish that the *upadeśika* [injunction] of the afternoon has only an optional sublation.
In the *Śrāddhakalpa*, in the section on the determination of the time for *śrāddha* (123),
there is an inconsistency: how then is it that in the *dvijāmi-śrāddha*, the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) is prescribed as the [primary] time?

Regarding the statement that "the *mudrā-śrāddha* is for one who has received instruction," it is replied: The primary *pārvaṇa* śrāddha, consisting of the feeding of Brahmins, is obligatory (*nitya*). That [obligatory rite] pertains exclusively to a performer who is of the twice-born (*dvija*) caste, and not to a performer who is a Śūdra;
for, by prohibiting the śrāddha consisting of the feeding of Brahmins for the latter, the *ām-śrāddha* (śrāddha with raw food) is prescribed as his obligatory duty.

If, even after setting aside the prohibition, the injunction for cooked food were to apply there as well, then an inequality would arise: namely, that in the case of a Śūdra there is a dependence on setting aside the prohibition, whereas in the case of the twice-born (dvija) there is no such dependence.
Thus, that which consists of feeding Brāhmaṇas—which is the primary *brāhmaya* and *pārśvala*—is of the nature of the twice-born.

The [śrāddha] pertaining to the agent is eternal (*nitya*). However, the *āma-śrāddha* (raw-food śrāddha), prescribed for the twice-born on account of causes such as the impossibility of cooking, is non-eternal (*anitya*). This being the case, the ritual properties (*dharma*) taught in the archetype (*prakṛti*), such as the feeding of Brāhmaṇas and so forth, must apply only to the eternal rite by virtue of that instruction, and not to any other.

Even for one who desires to perform the *śrāddha* on specific occasions, [the performance] must be considered obligatory (*nitya*), because of the contradiction between the connection of the obligatory and the non-obligatory (*nityānityasaṃyogavirodha*). Just as the prescribed elements such as the *dīkṣā*, *gīti*, and so forth, are seen to be constituent parts (*upasarjana*) of the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice— which is the *agniṣṭoma* form and is obligatory— and not of any other non-obligatory [form], or likewise [the elements] such as the purchase (*kraya*) and so forth.

The [rites] belong only to the eternal Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice which has soma as its substance, and not to that which is non-eternal or which has other substances as its medium. However, in the case of the non-eternal, they occur only by way of extension (atideśa). And in that non-eternal case, the others follow from the very rule "dvija-kāma-śrāddha. But for the Śūdra’s śrāddha, because it is non-occasional (anaimittika), [the rules do not apply].

Because it is eternal, it is established solely through direct instruction; thus, it is "instructional" (*aupadeśika*). This [instruction] sublates the previous alternative, which was based on the non-credibility of the twice-born, by virtue of being instructional. Therefore, this prior injunction—being rendered inconsistent by such a disparity, wherein it is mandatory in one case and optional in another—is [set aside].

It is only that specific object which is fit to be resorted to. And since no other alternative exists, [the ritual] abandons the *śūdra-śrāddha* and resorts to the *dvija-śrāddha* alone. This being the case, it is said:
"That *kutapa* cloth which is designated as superior to the midday [time], by the mere offering of food upon it, what is given becomes inexhaustible for the ancestors."

First: "Ignorance, Volitional Formations, Consciousness, Name-and-Form, the Six Sense Bases, Contact, Feeling, Craving, Grasping, Becoming, Birth, and Old Age and Death—these twelve are called the Links of Dependent Origination. Second: "Ignorance is the lack of knowledge regarding the truths; Volitional Formations are the karmic actions driven by that ignorance; Consciousness is the seed that enters the womb; Name-and-Form is the development of the body and mind; the Six Sense Bases are the completion of the faculties; Contact is the meeting of object, faculty, and consciousness; Feeling is the experience of pleasure, pain, or neutrality; Craving is the thirst for further existence; Grasping is the clinging to sense objects; Becoming is the formation of future karma; Birth is the arising of the aggregates; Old Age and Death are the decay and end of life. Third: "Ignorance is the root of all suffering; Volitional Formations are the causes of rebirth; Consciousness is the link that connects past and future; Name-and-Form is the foundation of the individual; the Six Sense Bases are the gateways of perception; Contact is the condition for sensation; Feeling is the basis for craving; Craving is the origin of grasping; Grasping is the fuel for becoming; Becoming is the cause of birth; Birth is the source of old age and death. Fourth: "Through the cessation of Ignorance, Volitional Formations cease; through the cessation of Volitional Formations, Consciousness ceases; through the cessation of Consciousness, Name-and-Form ceases; through the cessation of Name-and-Form, the Six Sense Bases cease; through the cessation of the Six Sense Bases, Contact ceases; through the cessation of Contact, Feeling ceases; through the cessation of Feeling, Craving ceases; through the cessation of Craving, Grasping ceases; through the cessation of Grasping, Becoming ceases; through the cessation of Becoming, Birth ceases; through the cessation of Birth, Old Age and Death cease. Fifth: "Thus, by the cessation of these twelve links, the entire mass of suffering comes to an end. This is called the cessation of Dependent Origination. Sixth: "One should contemplate these links as they arise and pass away, moment by moment. By seeing their true nature, one attains liberation. Seventh: "Ignorance is not a primary creator; it arises dependent upon conditions. All phenomena are likewise empty and devoid of self. Eighth: "Just as a lamp depends on oil and a wick to burn, so too do the links of existence depend on causes and conditions. Ninth: "If one can sever the chain of Ignorance, the subsequent links will naturally cease. This is the path to the cessation of suffering. Tenth: "Therefore, the wise should cultivate mindfulness and wisdom, and abandon all delusions. Only by realizing the truth of Dependent Origination can one reach the shore of Nirvāṇa. In the *Śrākalpa*, within the section on the determination of the times for *śrāddha*:
it is now deliberated whether the *śrāddhas* performed at each respective time are distinct or not.

Are the sentences concerning time injunctions for the production of an action, or are they injunctions of time regarding an action already produced? In this regard, although an injunction of the verbal root’s meaning (bhāvārtha) and an injunction of the sentence-meaning (vākyārtha) would result from enjoining a subordinate factor (guṇavidhāna), nevertheless, because the injunction transfers to the specific [time] and because of parsimony (lāghava), [it is the latter].

Since these are indeed injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*), they do not bring about a difference in the ritual action (*karmabheda*). Therefore, even when there are optional alternatives (*vaikalpika*) that occur simultaneously, performance takes place at one time or another, but not all at once. How much less, then, could there be separate performance for those occurring simultaneously? This is the case regarding the conjunction of times (*kālasamavāya*).

Only one *śrāddha* should be performed; for it is not accepted that there should be a repetition of the primary act (*pradhāna*) merely in accordance with the qualities of time for anyone. As for the repetition of the *homa* offerings in accordance with times such as evening and morning, that is due to the repetition of the occasion consisting of life as delimited by those specific desires.

To this it is replied: where there is a pure origination (of the substance) within the context of the mantra-application, there—in those sentences concerning the qualities—the injunction pertains to the quality alone, due to the recognition of that [substance]. Here, however, because there is no pure origination, and because there would be the fault of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) in an injunction of a qualified entity as a last resort, this [injunction] is indeed qualified, provided one does not assume a separate origination of the pure [substance].

Due to the omission of a specific injunction, there might be some distinction based on the quality [of the time]. However, because the Vedic texts prescribe a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), there is a distinction between the *śrāddha* for each respective time. Furthermore, since eclipses and the like serve as occasional causes (*nimitta*), the distinction therein is clear.
Therefore, it is established that when those specific times arrive, the corresponding *śrāddha* must be performed.

Now, a doubt arises regarding the conjunction of times (*kāla-samavāya*) and the conjunction of causes (*nimitta-samavāya*): among the various *śrāddha* rites belonging to those respective times and occasions, should only one be performed, or should they all be performed separately? Regarding this: in that case, when there is a single...

Since there is a prohibition against performing *śrāddha* [at the same time], it might follow that only one [should be performed]; to this it is replied: when many, or even two, have died at the same time, one should perform the cooking once by way of a single procedure (*tatra*), but perform the *śrāddha* offerings separately for each.
In the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*,
in the section on the Paribhāṣā of the *Parva-khaṇḍa* [580]:
"First for the one who has died previously, and then again for the second."
Then one should apply the third; this is the sequence for cases of combined derangement (sannipāta).

Thus, since Bhṛgu has stated that the performance of numerous *śrāddhas* with various occasions (*nānānimitta*) may take place on the same day, and since it has been established in such passages as "twelve days are recommended" that the performance of various *preta-śrāddhas* on a single day is permissible, [the rule] "not by one person... [is not contradicted].

Since this prohibition— "one should perform two *śrāddhas* on the same day, if possible"— is established as referring to cases where a single occasion for a *śrāddha* initiated by a *śrāddha*-inert (or ignorant) person coincides with a *vṛddhi* (prosperity) rite, the position that all [the rites] must be performed separately is adopted. As for the argument that, due to the identity of place and time, there is no perception of a distinction [between the occasions]—

It has been stated that the performance of subsidiaries such as the *prayāja* offerings is to be done once (*tantra*) when they are included within a single performance injunction; this is appropriate only for subsidiaries, however, and not even for independent primary rites. As for the incidental application (*prasaṅga*) of the two *darśa-pūrṇamāsa* sacrifices performed for the sake of a specific desired result (*kāmya*) to a rite performed for the sake of the unseen merit (*apūrva*), that too occurs only when there is identity of the ritual act.

It is appropriate [to say] that they are identical. For just as the two groups beginning with the Āgneya sacrifice are both the *kāmya-apūrva* (the unseen result of a desire-based rite) and the *nitya-apūrva* (the unseen result of an obligatory rite), so too are those two understood from their originative injunctions (*utpatti-vākya*) to be the same.

As for the conventional usage of distinction (*bheda-vyavahāra*) in that regard, it is based on the difference in cognition caused by the connection with limiting conditions (*upādhi*) in the form of the desired object (*kāma-rūpa*) or the occasioning cause (*nimitta-rūpa*). It rests upon the non-difference of the essence (*vasty-abheda*).

It is not based on a difference in the underlying entity (*vastu*). However, the unprecedented [result] (*apūrva*) is real because of the difference in qualification (*adhikāra*). Therefore, although this [difference] is conditional (*aupādhika*), it is investigated as having the characteristic of difference, considering that it brings about the differentiation of the *apūrva*.

Indeed, [this difference] is based on the perception of difference resulting from the coloring by the distinction between the various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) in the form of the respective meanings of the verbal roots.
It has been established that there is a distinction between the mental dispositions (*bhāvanā*) involved in sacrifice, gift-giving, and oblation. True;

however, in those cases, the distinction—conceived through the cognition of distinct verbal suffixes—is accepted as real because there is no subverting factor (*bādhaka*). In the present context, however, it is unreal, because there exists a subverting factor in the form of the apparent identity of the action produced by the originative injunction (*utpatti-śāstra*).

And because of the unity of the action, the optional [rites] are accomplished by means of the very same Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices performed for the sake of the former [obligatory purpose], even though there are many [optional rites] having distinct causes.
