When the performance is established as constant, no separate performance is carried out. However, when there is a break, because the previous [performance] is not accomplished by another [subsequent one], there is a performance of the other for that purpose. Or, let it be granted that there is some subtle difference in the ritual action (*karmabheda*) even within the Vedic tradition; yet that is distinct from other types of differences. It is itself—
It might be argued that someone who has approached a venerable person desires to request something else entirely.

To this it is replied: even when there is a plurality of actions, provided there is excellence of place, time, and agent, by performing them all together, the completion of all previous [obligations] is achieved simultaneously; for at that time, nothing is perceived [to remain unfulfilled].

There is a distinction, namely: "this is accomplished, this is not. Furthermore, it is accepted that even when there is a difference in the sacrifice (*yāga*), the ritual procedure (*tantra*) is performed with a single deity. This is as stated in the rule: "In the case of the *māmnāyya*, in dreams, crossing a river, rain, and upon seeing impurity (*amedhya*) or a corpse, it is the same"—wherein, when multiple instances of seeing impurity occur simultaneously as the occasion (*nimitta*), [the procedure is the same].

The sign (*nimitta*) has begun; "the mind is poor," thus it is said. When the end of the ritual occasion consisting of the recitation of this mantra has been reached, because there is no apprehension of any further distinction, the performance of my own ritual occasion is established as being in one part [of the whole].

Therefore, because there is no distinction made regarding the conjunction [of the new moon], the time, the place, the performer, or the deity when these coincide, the performance of the *śrāddha* must be carried out at that [conjunction].
This being the case, the *śrāddha* occasioned by the *saṃkrānti* (the sun’s passage into a new zodiacal sign) and that occasioned by the new moon (*amāvāsyā*)— which have been set forth...
One should form the intention: "I shall perform these [rites] together with the *mitrakas* by means of the *tantra*.
This concludes the determination of the time and the assembly (*samavāya*).
Thus [ends the work of] the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja, the illustrious Mahādeva, the lord of the office of the *yamastaka*. All...

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Time for Śrāddha," in the *Pariśeṣa-Śrāddhakalpa* of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by the learned Śrī Hemādri, the sovereign who brings about auspiciousness and is proficient in the sciences. ● ||1||

Therefore, with diligence, one should feed a lord of yogis who is devoted to knowledge during offerings to the gods and ancestors, rather than other brahmins who are ignorant.
"By a hundred forest-dwellers,
and by a hundred householders, [one] forest-dweller [is equaled]."
Among all yogas, the yoga of the great sound of the celibate student is distinguished as supreme.
Whether one is an atheist, a skeptic, or even a fool,
when it comes to the cause of giving, he is a master of yoga and a lord of creatures.

who feeds a meditator with food— whether he be a son, a grandson, or a great-grandson.

whoever knows even a little of the dharma of sacrifice, having properly relied upon the stages of life (āśrama) and social orders (varṇa), is considered by them to be a most excellent and supreme worthy recipient (satpātra).

Those who follow the conduct of great forest-dwellers—to them, "that" [state] has been previously described as "the light of lights," such is the meaning. This praise of the yogi is seen in the Śātātapa-smṛti; thus it is said.

From the *Brahmavaivarta*: "But those who are always established in right conduct (*vṛtta*), as well as the knowers (*jñānins*) and meditators (*dhyānins*),"— since this passage declares that only those knowers and meditators who are established in right conduct are to be fed.

"Knowledge" is the thorough establishment in the reality of the self and so forth; "concentration" is the contemplation of the formed and the formless. As stated in the Bhagavadgītā in the Mahābhārata:
"The yogi is superior to those who practice austerity, and he is considered superior even to those possessed of knowledge."
"And since yoga is superior to all these, therefore, O Arjuna, become a yogi."
Thus ends the description of the winds for yogins.
Now, elsewhere Chāgaleya states the fault of transgression for a yogin:
If one should bypass a yogin and instead worship a cowherd,
one does not obtain the fruit of that [worship], but rather causes one's own lineage to suffer.

"Gṛhamya" refers to one who performs [forbidden] acts. He does not obtain the fruit of that action. Likewise, "he would torment his own lineage" (magotraṃ) means that he would cause even his ancestors, born of his own family line, to suffer by making them miserable through the transgression (pratyavāya) produced by such improper conduct.
Likewise,
they bypass the practitioner and feed one another.

Both the giver and the eater go to hell along with their great kinsmen; it should be understood that here the descent into hell for both the giver and the eater is intended to apply when there is the intention of transgressing what is appropriate. Therefore, he says: "they cause one another to eat."

Now, the donor feeds the yogin with the intention: "Having been fed by me today, he will feed me in his own home. The eater likewise eats while conforming to that very same [intention]. Both of these possess the intention of transgressing the yoga. However, when it belongs to the donor alone—

If [the meat] was intended [for the guest], then there is no transgression for the eater. When a violation occurs through negligence regarding one's intention, it is merely a slight defect in the *śrāddha* rite; at that time, there is no falling into hell for anyone.
Vṛddhaśātātapa also says:
If one should feed a householder while bypassing a yogin, one does not obtain that fruit; rather, one would cause even heaven to fall.
He who remains only in the household and not in yoga is here called a "householder" (gṛhastha). [The phrase] "leading to heaven" refers, by ellipsis, to one's own group of ancestors.
Those who, bypassing yogins, worship one another [are thus described].
But those who give liquor shall go to hell along with their kinsmen.
Thus concludes the description of the faults incurred by a yogin through transgression.
Now, the state of being a yogin for householders and others is described.

In this context, what is called "union" (*yoga*) is, in its primary sense, a relationship characterized by the state of becoming one with the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Although it is innate and common to all individual selves (*kṣetrajña*), it is nevertheless [obscured] by beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*).
This [knowledge] is not for those who possess the recollection of "I" (ahaṃ-smṛti) due to the obscuration caused by the notion of difference; rather, it belongs only to the liberated.

And the means to this is the knowledge of the reality of the Self (ātmatattva-jñāna). Its means is also sacrifice (yāga), which consists of eight limbs beginning with restraint (yama) and ending with concentration (samādhi). This is based on the etymological derivation of the instrument-case (karaṇa-vyutpatti): "by this, the individual soul (jīva) is joined with the Supreme Self."

Or rather, by its primary sense, it is sacrifice (*yajña*); because of the authority of the scripture, even one who lives as a householder is a "sacrificer" (*yāgin*) when that [sacrifice] is his end.
And this is not a figurative usage, because sacrifice is the sole means; thus, the connection with yoga belongs only to the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*), not to the householder.
It is not so, because having become dispassionate toward objects that are seen to be more frequently marred by defects, [he attains it].

Even for one who possesses pride and ego, when that [knowledge] which transcends all human goals has arisen, a desire for it occurs. And when that [desire] exists, for the wise person who is capable of practicing its means, the practice of yoga is indeed appropriate because of their eligibility;
and for one who has practiced yoga correctly, there is liberation. And that—
In the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, in the section on the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa*,
[it is stated]: "For one who has occupied his time with the performance of duties pertaining to his own stage of life (*āśrama*), there is no opportunity for the practice of yoga."

Or rather, [it applies] to the *vāka* [stage], because even for a *bhikṣu*, there is the possibility of an occasion for it during the intervals between the performance of his obligatory duties. Nor is the practice of yoga useless for a householder, since yoga alone is the means to liberation for one who has entered the fourth stage of life (*turīyāśrama*). For they record in their tradition:
"One who has acquired wealth by righteous means, is devoted to the knowledge of reality, is fond of guests, performs ancestral rites,
and speaks the truth— even such a householder is liberated."

Moreover, it is heard that even householders such as Janaka, Jābāla, Vāmadeva, Prahlāda, and others attained liberation through the practice of yoga. And here, by the term "established in the knowledge of reality" (*tattvajñānaniṣṭha*), it should be understood that one is established in the knowledge of the true nature of the self (*ātmatattvajñāna*). By this, it follows that the restraints (*yama*) and other practices, which serve as the means for the knowledge of the true nature of the self, [are included] up to meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Even for one who has fallen from [his vow], there is no grief;
and so it is said in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"Whether they be householders, lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhika), peaceful forest-dwellers, or even ascetics..."
Yogis worship the Supreme Self through the self.

Householders and others are also yogins. This being the case, among householders and the like, those who possess the excellence of qualities such as the study of sacred texts (svādhyāya) and so forth are yogins; one should offer funeral rites (śrāddha) to those who stand before them.
Now, regarding that which is called the "Yati" (ascetic) who is distinguished by such [qualities], the rule for the Śrāddha is stated; and on this point Manu says:
"Some twice-born men are devoted to knowledge, and others likewise are devoted to austerity."

likewise, offerings to the gods (*havya*) and to the ancestors (*kavya*) should be given to all four [classes of people].

1.1 Furthermore, the consumption of honey and meat would result in the ascetic falling into an unrestricted state. To this it is replied: The injunction "one should feed" prescribes the act of feeding with honey and meat as a causal operation (*prayojakavyāpāra*) performed by the agent authorized for the *śrāddha* rite; it does not, however, prescribe such an act as an operation performed by the ascetic (*yati*) who is the person enjoined (*niyojya*) in the *śrāddha*.

Yama said:
That high-souled person by whom all lunar days, festivals, and celebrations have been abandoned is a guest for all living beings; they know the rest to be merely visitors.
A guest is called *atithi* because he is a renunciant (*yati*) who dwells for a time;
since he stays only temporarily, they know him as an *atithi*.
"Days of the lunar fortnight" (*tithi*) refers to the first day (*pratipad*) and so forth; "market days" (*paṇi*) refers to the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) and so forth;

"festivals" (*utsava*) refers to weddings and the like. The meaning is that he who, being devoted to the dharma of an ascetic, has renounced these—which are causes for obtaining special food—is a guest (*atithi*). "One observing a vow" (*vratau*) refers to a celibate student (*brahmacārin*).

The term "yati" refers to a wandering mendicant; it is only these two who possess the status designated as "guests" (*atithi*) among those following the dharma of prescribed rules, and not householders or forest-dwellers. Regarding those two [the latter], their designation as "visitors" (*abhyāgata*) is stated in the *Vāyu Purāṇa*.
The Vālakhilya and the ascetic are to be known as the lunar days (tithis) of pride;

The *vālakhilyas* are celibate students (*brahmacārins*). "Pacānaḥ" means "one who cooks," that is, a householder or a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*). Furthermore, there are two kinds of guests: those who arrive at midday and those who arrive in the evening.

Regarding this injunction to feed other invited Brahmins in another residence, it may appear as if it were contradictory to the feeding of the guest at the *śrāddha* site along with the principal guests; however, that too refers to a situation where it is impossible to find any other space in that same location.
Alternatively, this should be understood as referring to those Brahmins who are to eat after the *śrāddha* ceremony, distinct from the invited guests (*atithi*).

Even in that case, the "first" refers specifically to the one who partakes in the remnants (*ucchiṣṭa*) at the end of the *śrāddha* Brahmin's meal; whereas according to another view, it refers to those [who eat] in the house itself. Thus, in this context, the state of being a guest (*ātithya-bhāva*) is devoid of the specific characteristics of a formal guest.
By means of another method— namely, requesting food on account of his mother— he says ten times to the one who creates obstacles for the ancestral rite (*śrāddha*):
"A Brahmin who causes obstacles destroys the evil deeds of four [generations]."
Likewise, [I bow] to the Lord of the Lord of Food for those who desire food.
"For those desiring food" means for the ancestors (pitṛs) who are to be satiated at a Śrāddha or at a Śrāddha-aryapāka; that is the meaning.
Thus concludes the determination of the guest's status as a recipient of food in the row of the Śrāddha.

Now, in the event that such aforementioned Brahmins are unavailable, compassion is prescribed for the purpose of performing the Śrāddha even with fewer [guests]. Regarding this, Manu, having described the twice-born who are most worthy based on their knowledge and other qualities, says:
This is the primary rule for the offering of *havya* and *kavya*:
that one should bestow them upon those who are compassionate, self-conquered, and free from pride—this is how it has been practiced by the wise.
"This" refers to the *anantati* [the primary sequence]. "Principal" (*mukhya*) means primary. "Ritual procedure" (*kalpa*) means the rule (*vidhi*).
Regarding "the application in giving": "this," however, is what will be described. "Secondary" (*anukalpa*) means a subsequent arrangement (*anu-paścāt-kalpanam*);
the meaning is that it is performed in the absence of the primary. Previously, it was stated that this should be given for the sake of the principal. Hereafter—
In its absence, [one should give] to an *ullaghṛtagaya*; in the absence of such a person, to one who is *utkṛṣṭa*; and in the absence of even that, to someone [who is merely] *tamprāpya*.

In the *Pariśeṣa-khaṇḍa* of the *Caturvarga-cintāmaṇi*, he will state that [the gift] should be given to a learned man (*śrotriya*). Likewise, it was previously stated that it should be given to one who is not a relative (*asambandhin*).

Since it will be stated hereafter that "in the absence of those [heirs], it should be given to the relatives," this [act] is a praise, meaning that such compassion has been practiced by the wise. Thus it is said in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:

One should feed pure meditators among the monks who possess the "unnavel" (*anābha*) wisdom; but in their absence, one should feed those who are well-versed in the three Vedas and are celibate students (*brahmacārin*);
and in the absence of even these, one should feed even a householder who is restrained in speech.

"Bhikṣus" are ascetics who carry the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*), or forest-dwellers (*vānaprasthas*) who are meditative. "Udāmauna" means those unrelated to a donor, or those devoid of friendship and fire. First of all, it has already been established that the *bhikṣus* alone are to be understood here as the most excellent. Forest-dwellers are similar to them; of these—

In the absence of these, those who have reached the final stage of the vow of lifelong celibacy (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārin*) are the foremost among the Veda-knowers. In their absence, householders who possess the qualities of being a worthy recipient of the funeral feast (*paktipātra*) and so forth should be considered. These are the knowers of Brahman.
First, yogins should be honored by those of self-restraint during funeral rites (śrāddha);
in their absence, those who know the Vedas, and after them, those who merely recite them.
This great ritual procedure is to be applied; it is the means for attaining the vessel.

Even among householders, those who do not perform sacrifices but are knowers of Brahman (*brahmavid*) are the foremost. In their absence, those who "know the Veda" (*vedavit*), meaning those who understand the meaning of the Vedas. In their absence as well, those who are "merely reciters" (*pāṭhamātra*), who perform only the recitation of the Veda.

Even Vikāra, among those who know the Vedas, has uttered this praise: "He who, having studied the Veda, does not understand its meaning, is indeed a mere bearer of a burden, like a pillar carrying a load.
But he who knows it attains all prosperity; may we be such as have our sins shaken off by knowledge."

"Touched by impure things" means touched by substances, whether animate or inanimate, that have fallen from an impure place. "Stale" (śukta) has been explained previously. "Sour" (paryuṣita) means that which has remained overnight.

"Dvisvinam" means cooked twice. When that which has been prepared here by the act of cooking is placed back into water and cooked again until the covering cloth is removed, that is "dvisvinam. It does not refer to that which, having already been prepared, is merely set upon the fire again for the sake of maintaining its heat. "Pratyuṣṇam" [means while still warm].

This is because of the statement, "It should be my food. Furthermore, even when the middle [portion] is being softened again, it is not considered "twice-cooked" (*dviḥsvinna*). However, for those things such as rice-porridge (*raṇa*) whose accomplishment is well-known to occur through two acts of placing on the fire, since that cooking consists of only a single process regarding its constituent parts, there is no state of being "twice-cooked" even in that case.

‘Pagdigdha’ refers to that which has been dried out by the heat of a vessel due to the evaporation of its liquid portion. ‘Śradyātrale hita’ means licked at the front—that is, tasted by cats and the like—or having one part previously tasted by another. ‘Śarkarā’ is a specific type of white sugar. ‘Kauṭāḥ’ refers to ants and similar insects. ‘Pāṣāṇaḥ’ means stone.

*Dr̥ṣat* means stone. *Keśaḥ* means hair. That which has been defiled by these [hair and insects], having entered the mouth, becomes unfit to be eaten. *Mathitam* means churned curd. *Atilavaṇam* means excessively salty.
Those foods that have been prepared and processed—such as wheat flour products fried in oil or those dried from barley—are likewise [unfit].

Regarding foods such as snakes, cobras, and wandering spirits that have remained for a long time—even though they are "stale food" (*paryuṣita-bhakta*)—they are not considered defiled by [the rule of] "dwelling" (*vāsa*); thus it is said in the *Gaṇa*.
(1) Regarding "stale food," see *Gaṇa*.
(2) "Not defiled by dwelling" is likewise stated in the *Gaṇa*.
In the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, within the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* [section on miscellaneous topics], regarding legal procedure (*vyavahāra*):
those [meats] which are not [normally] eaten are called "prepared" (*siddha*) when they have been made ready; [this refers to] fresh salt...

"Prepared" means those mixed with salt while being watched by the eater. "Corrupted by speech" means those defiled by words in the form of censure and the like. "Defiled by the wicked" refers to those who have been rendered impure through sight, touch, and so forth, by pigs, crows, cocks, and the like, as well as by outcasts, heretics, and others.
"Eatables" (*bhakṣyāḥ*): Those foods over which a cloth is shaken—either to drive away flies, to cool them by fanning, or for some other incidental reason—are so designated. Manu says:

Food into which hair or insects have fallen, that which has been intentionally touched with the foot, that which has been looked upon by a killer of an embryo, and that which has been touched by a woman in her courses;
Food that has been pecked by a bird, food clearly seen by a dog, and especially food announced [for public consumption]— these are forbidden.
One should avoid partridge that is stale, the leavings of a Śūdra, meat not consecrated by ritual, rice boiled with sugar-cane juice, milk-rice, cakes, meat not prepared for sacrifice,
and the sacrificial food and oblations intended for the gods.

"Contaminated by hair and insects" (*keśakīṭāvapanna*) means touched by hair and insects. The mention of "hair" (*keśa*) is for the purpose of indicating [the inclusion of] eye-secretions and other impurities for up to nine nights; the mention of "insects" (*kīṭa*) is for the purpose of indicating small creatures such as worms and moths.

In the case of insects, clay and other such things defile only when dead, not while alive; however, [in the case of] those that are living, it is otherwise. "Intentionally" (*kāmataḥ*) means with prior awareness; since it is touched by the foot intentionally, there is no fault in what is touched through negligence (*pramāda*). A "feticide" (*bhrūṇahā*) is a killer of a Brahmin; by him it has been scrutinized—that is, carefully observed.

*Kiṃsaṃ* [is mentioned] for the sake of illustration; this implies other great sinners (*mahāpātakin*) as well. As for the prohibition regarding one touched [by such persons], it is established by the very injunction for bathing. *Udakyā* means a woman in her menses; the prohibition applies specifically to one touched by her, not to one merely looked upon. Even though the prohibition regarding one touched by a menstruating woman is established by the injunction for bathing itself, [the specific mention of her] serves to emphasize...

The section on determining the substances to be cast into the fire in the Māikalkalpa (811):
The touching and washing [of the vessel] is for the purpose of ensuring that even food touched by a bird is fit to be eaten; "patacī" refers to a bird.

From their conduct, "flesh-eaters" (kravyāda) are those such as vultures and the like, but not parrots, swans, and so forth. "Ghuṣṭā" refers to that which is given after crying out, "Let anyone who desires food eat! When it is given to one person while having been promised to another, the verbal root *pra-ti-jñā* is understood [in this context]. "Of the Śūdra" means belonging to a Śūdra.

*Mikam* refers to food. *Ucchiṣṭam* means what remains after eating. *Śamara* is boiled rice prepared with sesame seeds. *Mandya* (or *maṇḍaka*) is a specific kind of food made from wheat flour mixed with sesame, ghee, jaggery, and so forth, which is well known in the Sūrasena country. *Pāyasa* is boiled rice cooked with milk. *Apūpaiḥ* refers to [foods] without oil—

"Cooked" refers to a preparation of wheat. The word "in vain" (vṛthā) is understood in connection with all [the following] items. When food is prepared for one's own sake, rather than being dedicated to the gods, the ancestors, or guests, that is "in vain. "Unconsecrated" (anupākṛta) means meat that has not been offered. "Belonging to the gods" (daivāni) refers to things dedicated to the deities. "Sviṣṭakṛt" refers to what is intended for the deity.
They were prepared.
Yājñavalkya:
Likewise.
Meat that has not been honored, meat obtained in vain, that which is infested with hair or insects, that which is stale, defiled by excrement, touched by a dog, or cast away.
One should also avoid food that has been touched by the rising sun, that which is proclaimed as unfit, and that which is stale;
as well as food from a lizard, the leavings of a bird, or that which has been intentionally touched with the foot.

Just as I have [described] the impurity of food such as *apūpa* and *pūṣkṛta*: "That which is given with contempt after having been improperly cooked is *anarcitam*. 'Vṛthāmāṃsa' (meat prepared in vain) is that which is not intended for the gods;
that which is prepared solely for one's own sake is what is rejected by the ancestors and others."
Who would avoid it? "Touched by tomorrow" (*śvaspṛṣṭa*) means not touched [by others]. By way of designating a connection with another, that which is stale is called "leftover" (*śiṣṭa*).
[Variant reading: *kha*].
In the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*,
that is called "paryāyanam. In the reading *paryācāntam*, it means that which has been completely rinsed (*parigatam ācāntam*).

"Paryācānta" refers to that which is being eaten while a mouthful is being held. Regarding the reading "pārśvācāntam," it means that when one person sitting at the side has finished rinsing his mouth (ācānta), one should not eat until the interruption [of the meal] by ashes, water, or the like has been made. "Śakuna" is a carnivorous bird. It is a preparation of wheat cooked in oil.
Śakunī. Yama.
Likewise.
Likewise:
that which is touched by a woman in her menses, that which has been struck by a cow, that which has been touched by a crow or a cock, and that which is joined with a single hair; [these are impure].
He fed the twice-born according to the word of Dharmarāja.
Barley gruel, rice-and-pulse porridge, milk-rice, cakes, and fried pastries; food cooked on chaff, and even meat that has not been formally consecrated for sacrifice.
One should avoid all divine foods and sacrificial oblations; however, one should never employ a meal intended for me with a base or inferior dish.
Food that has been sneered at, treated with contempt, served without anger, or offered with fear— even from a guru— should not be eaten if it is devoid of the proper consecration.
That which is publicly proclaimed, that which is leftover, that which is accompanied by speech [of censure],
and that which is given without faith— these are not to be eaten by the twice-born.
One should not eat from a broken vessel, nor should one consume curd from a broken pot. Fortune (Lakṣmī) always makes her abode in pomegranates by day and in curds at night.

Gruels and similar items prepared for one's own sake are inedible. *Yavāgū* is rice-gruel that is not excessively boiled and is thin in consistency. *Sṛjīṣa* is the vessel used for cooking flour-based foods.
According to the *Smṛticandrikā*, *jī* refers to a small earthen pan; that which is cooked within it while situated in a heap of grain and so forth is [also considered inedible].
*Śravadhūnaṃ* means "with a cloth. *Dadhityaṃ* means "wood-apple" (*kapittha*). *Dhāmā* refers to parched barley.
[Thus say] Devala and Gautama.
They declare that food which has been touched by a menstruating woman, food pecked at by a parrot,
and food that is stale is unfit for consumption, with the exception of honey, meat, ghee, and molasses.

One should not eat with milk, nor sleep at night in a field from which the grain has been removed; one should not discard a garment when it is obtained, for milk is traditionally remembered as a purifier.
One should not consume substances such as oil-cakes from which the oil has been extracted, or buttermilk and the like, if they lack strength.
"Vilayana" refers to the scum of boiled rice.

Āpastamba: One should avoid fermented liquids, churned butter, oil-cakes, honey, and meat; black grain, the food of a Śūdra, and whatever else is not approved by him; as well as non-sacrificial food, falsehood, anger, and that by which anger is provoked.
One desiring mindfulness, intelligence, heaven, and wisdom should avoid these twelve things. Likewise:

Food that has been touched by one who is impure, or food that has become impure in nature, or food defiled by an impure Śūdra, is unfit for consumption. Furthermore, food in which there is hair, or which is otherwise pure but touched by impure things, or where there are insects or filth; or food stepped upon by a foot, or seen by a dog, a cat, or a cook, is unfit for consumption.
Or if one who is eating is defiled by grief, or a dog or a Śūdra should touch him, or he should touch water that has not been purified.
In the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa*:
"Or, in whatever worlds one might be born, if one should offer the leavings without rising, or sip water for purification (*ācamana*) after having spat out [the mouthful]."

In a place where they would give food that has been covered by cows, or by other impure things; likewise, one should not eat food from a market stall, nor should one consume the juices of meat, honey, or salt.

Having discarded oil and ghee, one should employ [other substances]. One may eat food prepared in water that has been kept overnight, as well as other kinds of non-edible grain such as *śuka*; furthermore, parched grain, rice, *karambha*, tree-born vegetables, meat, flour, curd, trees, medicinal herbs, forest plants, roots, fruits, and semen—these are for restricted use.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state: Among those [drinks],
one should avoid those that are unfit for drinking, as well as those touched by a drunkard, a eunuch, a Caṇḍāla, a Pukkasa, a woman in her courses, or one afflicted with leprosy.
Likewise:

there is no prohibition here against food that has been cooked twice, nor that which is parched, nor that which is stale, with the exception of colored liquids, sour gruel, one's own bodily excretions, curd, molasses, wheat, barley, and preparations made from flour.
Hārīta says that [food] should be from one who is auspicious and has a face like the sun;

it should not be from a woman in her menses, nor from a loose woman, nor from one who is angry, nor from one with soiled clothing, nor from another's wife, nor should it be stale, nor raw, nor decomposed, nor anything else except for molasses, flour-cakes, and honey.
Oil cooked in *ramataila* and other such substances is not forbidden for drinking or bathing, nor is it considered contemptible. Gautama states:
Food constantly fallen into by hair or insects, or touched by the foot of a woman in her menses or a black bird, is unfit to be eaten.

Vasiṣṭha says that for one who has not attained self-restraint, cow's milk, curd, vegetables, roots, fruits, meat, and honey are not to be considered fit for consumption if they have been looked upon with a corrupted mind.
Furthermore, even that which has been prepared and kept overnight is permissible for one who is alone.
In the *Śrāddhakalpa*, the section defining substances to be offered:
That which is stale, that which is corrupted by its nature, that which is naturally impure, and furthermore, that which is cooked again, raw, or cooked with dregs—these may be offered at will.
But one should consume what has been sprinkled with [water] by him. Likewise:
"The leavings of one's teacher are not to be eaten; nor that which is left over, or defiled by leavings, or containing hair or insects."
And [food] infested by insects.
Bṛhaspati;
Yama.
A twice-born man should not eat food, whether it be solid or soft, that is forbidden by the scriptures,
nor meat that is censured, nor even various kinds of auspicious things that have been declared as semen by those who discourse on Brahman and are condemned by them.
Whether it be ghee or oil, if a Brahmin has not sipped water after eating,
Yama will consume that very morsel for you along with the cattle.
He who eats food from which the seasoning and salt have been removed stands as a protector over the donor; having eaten such food, he consumes sin.
Whatever may be given by one hand, or even held in one hand—
be it oil, salt, water, or milk-rice (pāyasa)— [is not accepted].
The word "we" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. Since that food was brought by her alone out of fear of one whose wealth is compassion,
likewise, whatever Śaudra restraint was brought by the hand— that too, O Śūdra, was brought by the pure.

It has been served; or rather, it is "praudra," meaning it has been inhabited by a *śūdra* and is thus unfit for a *śrāddha*. Furthermore, whatever food such as rice and so forth was brought for that purpose when asked, "Let this be brought for that purpose," that too is *praudra*.

In the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*,

it is stated that food which has come into contact with a person of low caste (*parapākadhara*), even if it is mixed with nectar-like substances and the like, becomes defiled through that contact; one should treat it as if it were the leavings of a *śūdra*.
Thus end the foods to be avoided. Now, regarding these foods declared as forbidden, certain exceptions are provided.
On this point, Manu says:
Likewise:
among all foods to be eaten, curd is produced from everything;
and those things which are prepared with auspicious flowers, roots, and fruits [are also permitted].

Whatever food, whether solid or soft, contains oil or fat and is not otherwise censured, may be eaten even if it has stood overnight; likewise, all remnants of sacrificial oblations (havis) may be eaten at any time.
Even if it has been stored for a long time, the twice-born may eat the first-fruits of barley,
wheat, and all products derived from milk.

Products derived from curd— such as whey (*udaśvit*), honey, *kināṭaka*, and *kūrcaka*— are called "sour-clarified" (*praśukra*). These are substances that, although originally sweet in taste, become excessively sour due to the lapse of time or through contact with other substances.

However, those such as pomegranates, emblic myrobalans, and citrons which are sour by their very nature are not [merely] called "sour" [in this context], nor are those such as mangoes and the like that have not yet reached ripeness;

for this term "sour" (*śukra*) refers specifically to the state of acidity (*amlaparyaya*). And among those [fruits], only those that are sour by virtue of time [i.e., through ripening] are [intended].

Having prohibited [the use of meat] by means of other substances such as roots and so forth, those mixed with them are permitted; and thus it has been stated by Gautama: "Only [meat] that is not dedicated [to a deity].
It is not [otherwise].

Having mixed [the soma] with water, the process of infusion is called *abhiṣava*; those [substances] which are infused together with flowers and so forth [are also included]. "Edible" (*bhakṣya*) refers to parched grains (*dhānā*) and cakes (*śaṣkulī*). Food that is solid and clear, such as boiled rice (*odana*) and the like, is also [included].
That which is not censured, which is endowed with fragrance, color, and flavor, and likewise provided with oiliness, may be eaten even if it has stood overnight.
The Section on the Determination of Substances to be Offered in the Śrāddhakalpa.

Even though the remnant of the oblation (*haviḥśeṣa*) is mixed with clarified butter (*abhighāraṇa-sneha*), it is taken separately for the sake of showing respect. "Long-standing" means having been set aside for two or three nights. "Produced from barley and wheat" refers to cakes, *makkā*, and so forth; even if they have not been cooked by fire.
"Edible food": "derivatives of milk," meaning modifications such as curd, buttermilk, and so forth. Yājñavalkya [states]:
"Food that has become stale may be eaten, provided it is not oily and has not been kept for a long time."
Nor here are there transformations of wheat, barley, or cow products.
Bṛhaspati;
likewise Vasiṣṭha.
One should eat curd, boiled rice, and even molasses produced from curd; it is stated in the Śruti that food cooked with ghee should be eaten along with these.
All preparations derived from barley and wheat, as well as those that are unwholesome,
and foods such as *rāga*, *khāḍa*, and *śukta* that have become stale, should be avoided.
Cakes, parched grain flour, fried grains, and *avaṭaka* and *maktra*; vegetables, meats, and *pūpa*, as well as thin rice gruel and thick rice porridge here.

Barley gruel, milk-rice, and whatever else is mixed with curd—all of these may be eaten even if they have stood overnight, provided they have not turned sour; however, one should avoid that which has become sour.

One should avoid cakes, parched grains, flour-mash, *makku*, meat-balls, oil, milk-rice, and vegetables that are not accompanied by meat; as well as other products made from wheat-flour, except for those prepared with ghee. Thus says Paiṭhīnasi.
One may eat stale food that has been sprinkled with ghee or clarified butter;
for those things that arise from such sources as stale food possess the singular nature of serving human ends, and thus they do not constitute an obstacle to the Śrāddha rite.
Thus far. In the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, in the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa*, [chapter] 60.

One should not offer food that is hot, nor sweat-laden, nor cooked under the sky; for it is prescribed that one should begin the cooking on the very day of the *śrāddha*, and because there is no possibility of the food being merely stale or otherwise impure.
Regarding the prohibition stated by Yama that one should not eat food that is not fit for sale:
"Cakes, fermented grain-drink, parched grains, *takra*, curd, clarified butter, and honey—
these may be eaten during the Puṣya asterisms, provided they are not the residue from a vessel."
This [prohibition] applies to substances such as buttermilk and the like, which are distinct from cakes, meat, and parched grain, and for which the possibility of consumption arises;
as Manu and Viṣṇu have stated.
*Udhanas*, *Devakhas*:
these are the exceptions to the prohibition against forest-dwellers.
Now, the characteristics of water fit for consumption:

it is clear, free from impurities, situated on the ground, and free from thirst-inducing qualities; it should not be turbid in its middle, and it should be endowed with pleasant fragrance, color, and taste.
Just as water on the ground is pure where a cow would not feel thirst, and likewise when it is not pervaded by impurity, so too is water situated upon a stone.

Thus, just as a universal form (*ākṛti*) is perceived in a single individual (*vyakti*), so too is the status of being one's own Veda (*svādhyāyatva*) found in each and every branch (*śākhā*); consequently, regarding the injunction "one's own Veda is to be studied," it is stated that one should effect the performance of rituals by means of the Veda to be studied, and thus the Veda serves the purpose of bringing about the knowledge of ritual action.

Because it is being prescribed as such, it is understood that one should study only a single Veda. Why, then, is there the mention of "other Vedas" in statements such as "having studied the Vedas" or "having studied two Vedas"?
We reply: because there is a mutual expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*) regarding ritual action within the different Vedas, the various Vedas are required for the comprehension of rituals.

According to the *Mīmāṃsā*, for a single person, there is no requirement to study multiple Vedas; however, even within a single Veda, when one moves to another recension (*śākhā*), rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma are understood to possess their complete set of constituent elements (*dharmaka*) independently of other recensions. Therefore, because the ritual action is identical, the restriction to the study of a specific recension within a single Veda results in the threefold division of the recensions (*śākhā-trikampa*).
Regarding this, the teachers have said: "The study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) does not mean the mastery of only a single recension (*śākhā*), for many recensions are included;

and since those [recensions] which share the same purpose are variations of the same form, there will be a unity of ritual action.
